content: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the most common microorganism associated with respiratory infections in individuals with cystic fibrosis. Retrospective studies have suggested that implementing an aggressive strategy of administering intravenous anti-pseudomonal antibiotics at regular intervals, regardless of the presence of symptoms, may improve survival rates. The objective of this review was to determine whether an elective (regularly scheduled) intravenous antibiotic regimen, as opposed to a symptomatic (as-needed) regimen, leads to improvements in clinical outcomes and survival rates in people with cystic fibrosis. Additionally, the review aimed to identify any adverse effects associated with the elective use of intravenous antibiotics, such as the potential for increased development of antibiotic-resistant organisms. To address these questions, a search was conducted using the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group Trials Register. This register includes references obtained from comprehensive electronic database searches, manual searches of relevant journals, and conference abstract books. The most recent search of the register was performed on March 15, 2012. The review included all randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared elective intravenous antibiotic regimens with symptomatic regimens, regardless of the duration or dosage. Studies involving individuals with cystic fibrosis of any age or disease severity were considered. Both authors of the review independently assessed the eligibility and quality of the trials and extracted the relevant data. The search identified four studies, but only two studies, involving a total of 79 participants, met the inclusion criteria and were included in the review. However, differences in the design and objectives of these studies prevented the pooling of data for meta-analysis. Neither of the included studies demonstrated significant differences in clinical outcomes between the groups receiving elective and symptomatic antibiotic regimens. The authors concluded that the available evidence is insufficient to support the superiority of elective intravenous antibiotic administration over symptomatic administration, despite its widespread use in clinical practice. Furthermore, the potential risks associated with elective antibiotic use, such as the development of resistant organisms, have not been adequately evaluated. The small number of participants in the included studies limits the reliability of the findings, and the results should be interpreted with caution. The authors emphasized the need for a well-designed, adequately powered, multicenter randomized controlled trial to address these issues comprehensively. While this review will no longer be regularly updated, the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group will continue to conduct searches every two years. If relevant new trials are identified in the future, the review will be updated accordingly.
